items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place, pointing at yourself to introduce who you are. You want to say "I'm a student." You've got the words — 私[わたし] for *I*, 学[がく]生[せい] for *student* — but how do you glue them together so it sounds like a real sentence and not two nouns dropped on the floor? That glue is は, the topic marker.

は is the very first particle most learners meet, and for good reason: it's how Japanese says "okay, here's what I'm talking about — now let me tell you something about it." You name your topic, stick は after it, and then make your comment.

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]です。
```

*I'm a student.*

That's the whole shape. 私[わたし] is the topic, は marks it, and 学[がく]生[せい]です is the comment about it. Notice one thing right away that trips everyone up the first week: this particle is written with the character は but pronounced *wa*, not *ha*. That's normal — it's a historical spelling quirk, and it only happens when は is doing this topic job.

## How it works

The structure is simple: **Noun + は + comment**. The noun is what you want to talk about. は announces it as the topic. Everything after は is your statement about that topic.

Think of は as drawing a line: "As for this thing — here's the deal." A loose but useful translation of は is "as for." *As for me, student.* Clunky in English, perfectly natural in Japanese.

```jp
これは本[ほん]です。
```

*This is a book.*

Here これ (this one) is the topic, and 本[ほん]です (is a book) is the comment. The comment doesn't have to be short, and it doesn't have to be a です sentence either — but everything you know so far ends in です, so that's what we'll lean on.

You can make the topic a person's name, a pronoun, or any noun at all:

```jp
彼[かれ]は学[がく]生[せい]です。
```

*He is a student.*

```jp
あなたは学[がく]生[せい]です。
```

*You are a student.*

The pattern never changes based on what the topic is. は itself doesn't conjugate, doesn't shift form, doesn't care whether the topic is singular or plural. It's one of the most stable pieces of machinery in the whole language — it just sits there marking the topic, every single time.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest thing to internalize: は marks the **topic**, not necessarily the grammatical subject. In simple sentences these overlap so much that you won't feel the difference yet, but keep the word "topic" in your head. It'll matter soon.

Because は sets up "what we're talking about," Japanese loves to drop things once the topic is clear. If it's obvious you're talking about yourself, you can leave off 私[わたし]は entirely and just say 学[がく]生[せい]です. That's not lazy — it's how the language breathes. The topic, once established, doesn't need repeating.

> は is pronounced *wa* when it's the topic marker, even though it's written with the character for *ha*. When は is just part of a word (not a particle), it's read *ha* normally. This one spelling quirk confuses everyone at first — you're not misreading it.

One more caution: don't sprinkle は onto every noun in a sentence. A sentence usually has **one** topic. Marking two different nouns with は in the same breath will sound strange unless you're deliberately drawing a contrast, which is a move you'll learn later.

## Casual speech

Good news here: は as a topic marker stays は in casual speech. It doesn't contract or drop the way some particles do. What changes around it is the *comment* — casual speakers often drop the です at the end.

```jp
これは本[ほん]。
```

*This is a book. (casual)*

Same topic, same は, just a more relaxed comment with です chopped off. So the particle you're learning now carries straight over into casual speech unchanged — one less thing to relearn later.

## Contrast

You haven't met other particles yet, so there's nothing to line は up against just now. But here's the tease worth holding onto.

Very soon you'll meet が, the subject marker. It looks like it does the same job as は — and the difference between は and が is one of the genuinely hard, genuinely famous puzzles in Japanese. The short version: は says "as for X, here's the news," while が points a spotlight and says "*X* is the one." You don't need that distinction yet, but plant a flag here, because when が arrives, the first question will be "wait, how is this different from は?"

You'll also soon meet を for marking the object of a verb, and の for linking nouns together. All three live in the same neighborhood as は — little particles doing the quiet structural work — but は is the one that sets the stage for everything else.

Recap: name your topic, add は (say it *wa*), then comment. That's the backbone of the Japanese sentence, and you'll use it in nearly everything you ever say.
caution_notes: は as a topic marker is pronounced wa, not ha, even though it's written with the ha character.
は marks the topic (what you're talking about), which is not always the same as the grammatical subject.
Use only one は per sentence; marking two nouns with は sounds odd unless you mean to contrast.
Once the topic is clear, Japanese often drops it entirely — you don't need to repeat 私は every sentence.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing outside the theater with someone you like, the evening light going soft, and there's a movie you both keep mentioning. You don't want to *command* them to go — that feels heavy. You want to float the idea gently, leave the door open for them to say yes. Japanese has a beautiful move for exactly this: you phrase the invitation as a *negative* question.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか。
```

*Won't you watch a movie with me?*

Literally that's "won't you watch?" — and that softness is the whole point. By asking the negative, you're quietly signaling that a "no" is perfectly okay, which paradoxically makes people much more likely to say yes.

## How it works

The recipe is simple: take a verb, get its polite stem, and attach ませんか. You already know the polite negative ません (the "doesn't / won't" form). All you're doing is sticking a か on the end to turn that negative statement into a question.

Start from the polite form ます, swap it for ません, then add か:

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか。
```

*I watch a movie. / Won't you watch a movie?*

The pattern works with any verb the same way. Here's an invitation to have some tea:

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]にお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みませんか。
```

*Won't you have some tea with me?*

Notice how naturally 一[いっ]緒[しょ]に (together) rides along with this pattern. Invitations are almost always about doing something *with* someone, so 一[いっ]緒[しょ]に shows up constantly — think of them as travel companions.

And because it's a question, in speech your voice rises at the end, and in writing you'll often see a question mark even though か already does that job:

```jp
今日[きょう]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか？
```

*Won't you watch a movie today?*

## Rules and exceptions

This is polite, invitation-flavored language. The ます part means you're already being polite, so ませんか is safe with people you don't know well, and warm rather than stiff with people you do.

Watch out for one trap: ませんか as an *invitation* is not the same as an ordinary negative question about facts. Context and intonation carry the difference, but as a learner, assume the "won't you...?" invitation reading whenever you're proposing an activity.

> ません on its own is just "doesn't / won't" — a flat negative statement. It's only the added か, plus an activity you'd plausibly do together, that turns it into an invitation. 映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ません means "I don't watch movies"; 映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか means "won't you watch a movie (with me)?"

Also, don't reach for the plain negative here. 見[み]ない is the casual "don't watch," but you can't just tack か onto it and get this same polite invitation flavor — ませんか is a set, polite package. Keep it whole.

## Casual speech

Among close friends, people often drop the polite machinery entirely and invite with a plain negative plus a rising tone:

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ない？
```

*Wanna watch a movie?*

That final 見[み]ない？ with the voice lifting up does the same social work as 見[み]ませんか — it's just stripped down and intimate. Same idea for tea: 一[いっ]緒[しょ]にお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]まない？ is the buddy-level version of 飲[の]みませんか. Use the ませんか form until you know the relationship is casual enough; overshooting into casual too early reads as presumptuous, while polite is never wrong.

## Contrast with ましょう

You already met ましょう — "let's / shall we." Both ませんか and ましょう invite, so what's the difference? It's all about how much of a "no" you're leaving room for.

ましょう assumes you're both basically on board and just seals the plan. ませんか opens the door and lets the other person decide — it's the more considerate first move.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ましょう。
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか。
```

*Let's watch a movie (together). / Won't you watch a movie with me?*

A natural conversation often runs *through* both: you offer with ませんか, they say yes, and then you lock it in with ましょう. So they're not rivals — they're two beats of the same dance. Reach for ませんか when you're testing the waters, ましょう when the water's already warm.

Recap: verb stem + ませんか is your gentle, polite "won't you...?" invitation, softer than ましょう because it hands the choice to the other person. Hold onto that softening instinct — it comes back when we meet てください, where the tone you pick changes a request from an order into a favor.
caution_notes: ませんか is a polite, set invitation form — don't tack か onto the plain negative (見ない) and expect the same polite flavor.
ません alone is just a flat negative ('doesn't/won't'); it only becomes an invitation with か plus an activity you'd do together.
Use ませんか until you know the relationship is casual enough — polite is never wrong, but casual too early sounds presumptuous.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting in a quiet room and something moves in the corner. You want to say it out loud — "a cat!" — but not as the topic of a conversation, just pointing at the plain fact that a cat is *there*. This is the moment が was built for.

が is the subject marker: the little word that tags **who or what is actually doing the verb or being the thing**. Where は steps back and says "as for this, here's my comment," が leans in and points: *this one, right here, is the one.*

```jp
猫[ねこ]がいる。
```

*There's a cat.*

Notice there's no "as for" flavor here. You're not commenting on the cat as an already-known topic — you're announcing it. が does that announcing work.

## How it works

The structure is as simple as it looks: **Noun + が + Predicate**. The noun before が is the subject — the thing that exists, acts, or is described by whatever comes after.

The clearest place to feel が is with question words. When you ask *who* or *what* is doing something, you almost always reach for が, because you're asking the listener to fill in the unknown subject.

```jp
誰[だれ]がいる。
```

*Who's there?*

You can't make 誰[だれ] a topic — you can't comment on something you don't know yet. So は is off the table, and が steps in naturally. This is the single most reliable が instinct you can build: **question-word subjects take が.**

And the answer comes back with が too, because the answer is the newly-identified subject:

```jp
彼[かれ]がいる。
```

*He's there.*

が works the same way for existence and possession. When you're stating that something simply *exists* or that you *have* it, the thing that exists is marked with が.

```jp
お金[かね]がある。
```

*There's money. / I have money.*

Same shape every time: the thing being pointed at, then が, then the predicate. You don't conjugate が or change it — it's one fixed syllable doing one job.

## Rules and exceptions

The trap almost every learner falls into is reaching for が when they mean a general topic. If you're talking *about* yourself as the subject of an ongoing conversation, は is usually what you want. が is for the *new*, the *specific*, the *answer to a question* — the piece of information that wasn't already on the table.

> When a question word like 誰[だれ] or 何[なに] is the subject, use が, never は. "As for who?" is not a sentence.

There's a mirror rule that surprises people: the *answer* to a が question also takes が, but if you then shift to talking about that person generally, you switch back to は. The particle tracks what's new versus what's settled, not the grammar of the word itself.

> が marks the subject, but not every subject wears が. Once something becomes the known topic of the conversation, it often trades が for は.

## Casual speech

が itself doesn't contract — it's already a single clean syllable, so there's nothing to shorten. But in fast, casual speech, people often just *drop* it entirely when the meaning is obvious.

```jp
今[いま]、猫[ねこ]がいる。
猫[ねこ]いる。
```

*Right now, there's a cat. / A cat, there is.*

The first line is the full, neutral form. The second is what a friend might actually say pointing across the room — が gone, meaning intact. This dropping is casual only; in careful or polite speech, keep the が in.

## Contrast

Here's where が earns its keep against は, the topic marker you already know. Swap one for the other and the *feeling* of the sentence changes completely.

```jp
彼[かれ]がいる。
彼[かれ]は来[く]る。
```

*HE's the one who's here. / As for him, he'll come.*

The first line answers "who's here?" — が spotlights 彼[かれ] as the new, specific subject. The second uses は to set 彼[かれ] up as the topic and then comments about him. が points a finger; は sets a stage.

And against を, the direct object marker: を marks *what the action lands on*, while が marks *who does the action*. In a fuller sentence they'd sit on opposite sides of the verb — the doer in が, the done-to in を. For now, just hold the split: が is the actor, を is the target.

That's the whole core: が points at the subject, especially when it's new information or an answer to *who* or *what*. Hold onto this feeling — it comes back the moment we meet の and start linking nouns together.
caution_notes: When a question word like 誰 or 何 is the subject, use が — never は.
が marks new or specific subjects; once something becomes the known topic, it usually switches to は.
In casual speech が is often dropped entirely, but keep it in polite or careful sentences.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place for dinner, and the food is genuinely great. Your friend asks why you're going back for a third helping — and you want to say *because it's delicious*. But hold on: you don't have adjectives like "delicious" yet in your toolkit, so let's pick a reason you *can* say. Your friend asks why you're not drinking the beer, and the honest answer is: *because I'm a student* (and, let's say, too young). That "because" is から.

から is the workhorse "because" of Japanese. You take your reason, say it as a full sentence, and stick から on the end. That's the whole trick — no rearranging, no special verb form. The reason comes first, then から, then (often) the result.

## How it works

The structure is refreshingly flat: **a full clause + から**. Whatever sentence states your reason, you just append から to it.

Because the clause in front is a complete sentence, it can end in a verb, an adjective, a noun + です, whatever — から doesn't care. Here's a noun-predicate reason (someone *is* something):

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]ですから。
```

*Because I'm a student.*

Notice から sitting right after です. That's the polite pattern, sometimes listed as ですから — but it's really just です (the word that works like *is/am/are*) plus から glued on. Nothing new to memorize.

You can put the reason and the result in one breath. Reason first, から, then the consequence:

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいですから、昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]は肉[にく]です。
```

*Because I'm busy today, lunch is meat.*

Here the reason ends in the い-adjective 忙[いそが]しい ("busy"). から attaches straight to it — again, no reshaping the word. The comma after から is just breathing room; it's optional.

You can also flip the order. Say the result, then tack the reason on afterward as its own sentence ending in から:

```jp
昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]は肉[にく]です。忙[いそが]しいですから。
```

*Lunch is meat. Because I'm busy.*

This after-the-fact version is extremely common in speech — you blurt the point, then justify it. Both orders mean the same thing.

## Rules and exceptions

The big thing to internalize: から attaches to a **whole clause**, not to a noun by itself. English lets you say "because of the rain," gluing "because" onto a noun. Japanese から can't do that alone — it needs a real predicate in front. So you say 寒[さむ]いですから ("because it's cold"), not 寒[さむ]さから for "because of the cold."

You have a choice of politeness on the clause before から. Both of these are fine:

```jp
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いですから。
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いから。
```

*Because it's cold today.* (polite / plain)

The first keeps です for a polite tone; the second is the plain form. Here's the useful rule of thumb: match the clause before から to the formality of the sentence you're in. In a polite conversation, ...ですから feels smoother; among friends, the plain ...から is normal.

> から carries a slightly *subjective*, personal-reason flavor — it's *your* reason, sometimes with a hint of insistence. That's fine in most speech, but be aware that leaning on it hard ("...から！") can sound like you're pushing your excuse. When you want a softer, more neutral "because," Japanese has another tool (see the closing note).

One more trap: don't confuse this reason-から with the から that means "from" (a starting point). Same three sounds, totally different job. The "from" one attaches to nouns (a place, a time); the "because" one attaches to a clause. Context and what's in front of it tell them apart.

## Casual speech

In casual Japanese, you mostly just drop the です and keep the plain clause + から:

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいから。
```

*Because I'm busy today.*

You'll also hear だから standing alone at the start of a reply — literally "because (it) is" — used like "that's why" or, with attitude, "like I said." And a blunt だから何[なに]？ means "so what?" These are set phrases built from the same だ + から; you don't need to produce them yet, just recognize them.

## Contrast

You haven't learned any sibling patterns yet, so there's nothing to swap から against inside your current toolkit — which actually makes this the cleanest possible time to lock in one idea: **から = reason, and it lives at the end of the reason clause.** Reason, then から, then result. Get that shape into your ear now.

The only contrast worth flagging is the internal one from the rules section — reason-から (clause + から) versus from-から (noun + から). Keep them mentally in separate drawers.

Because you have this now, a whole category of sentences opens up: any time you can state a fact, you can turn it into a reason. Lock in the shape — reason clause, then から — because the very next "because" you meet, ので, lives in exactly the same space but sounds softer and more matter-of-fact. When you learn it, you'll define it against today's から.
caution_notes: から attaches to a whole clause with a real predicate, never to a bare noun the way English 'because of' can.
Match the politeness of the clause before から to the sentence around it: ...ですから in polite speech, plain ...から among friends.
Don't confuse reason-から (clause + から) with the から that means 'from' (noun + から); they look identical but attach to different things.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at your friend's place and their little sister is asleep on the couch. Someone turns the music up and you want to gently explain *why* everyone should keep it down — not bark an order, just point at the reason. In Japanese, the soft way to lay a reason on the table is ので.

You already have から for "because." ので lives in the same room, but it wears softer shoes. It presents the reason as a plain fact of the situation rather than as your personal push, which makes it perfect for explanations, apologies, and polite requests.

```jp
赤[あか]ちゃんですので、こちらはどうですか。
```

*It's a baby, so how about over here?*

## How it works

The core move is dead simple: take a clause in its **plain form** (the dictionary-style, non-polite form of a verb, adjective, or です), and stick ので on the end. The whole thing means "because [clause]."

With a plain verb, you just attach it directly.

```jp
明日[あした]、病[びょう]院[いん]ので、今日[きょう]は家[いえ]にいます。
```

*Because I have the hospital tomorrow, today I'm staying home.*

With an い-adjective, same deal — the adjective is already plain, so ので slots right on.

```jp
これは安[やす]いので、これにします。
```

*This one's cheap, so I'll go with this one.*

Here's the one spot that trips everyone up the first week — that's normal. With **nouns and な-adjectives**, the plain form of です is だ, but before ので that だ becomes **な**, not だ. So it's `noun + な + ので`, never `noun + だ + ので`.

```jp
彼[かれ]は医[い]者[しゃ]なので、こちらがいいです。
```

*He's a doctor, so this way is better.*

```jp
父[ちち]は今[いま]、病[びょう]気[き]なので、私[わたし]が行[い]きます。
```

*My father is sick right now, so I'll go.*

Notice 病[びょう]気[き] (a noun/な-type word here) takes な before ので. Say it out loud a few times — 医[い]者[しゃ]なので, 病[びょう]気[き]なので — and let the な feel automatic.

## Rules and exceptions

The big constraint: ので points at the reason, and the reason clause comes **first**. You don't lead with the result. The shape is always `[reason]ので、[result]`.

> ので attaches to the **plain** form even when your main sentence is polite. So you get 病[びょう]気[き]なので、行[い]きます — plain before ので, polite です/ます at the very end. Mixing plain-then-polite like this is correct and normal.

Because ので frames things as objective fact, it clashes with strong personal commands and blunt opinions. If you're barking an order or insisting on your own will, ので feels too soft and から fits better. For explanations and polite requests, ので is your friend.

One more: don't drop the な with noun sentences. 学[がく]生[せい]ので is a classic beginner slip; it must be 学[がく]生[せい]なので.

## Casual speech

In fast, casual speech ので often squeezes down to んで. It means exactly the same thing — it just sounds more relaxed and spoken.

```jp
今日[きょう]は病[びょう]気[き]なんで、うちにいます。
```

*I'm sick today, so I'm staying home. (casual)*

You'll hear んで constantly in conversation, especially tacked onto a light apology or excuse. It's not rude, just informal — keep the full ので for writing and polite situations.

## Contrast

Here's the pairing that matters. You know から; both から and ので mean "because." The difference is attitude.

- から pushes: it's *your* reason, and it can carry a bit of "so there." It happily sits under commands and strong opinions.
- ので lays a fact down gently: it's just how the situation is. It softens requests and apologies.

Swap them in a request and you can feel it:

```jp
安[やす]いので、これにします。
```

*It's cheap, so I'll go with this one. (calm, matter-of-fact)*

```jp
安[やす]いから、これにします。
```

*It's cheap, so I'll go with this one. (a touch more "because I say so")*

Same information, different temperature. When you want to sound considerate — to a teacher, a station worker, anyone you're being polite with — reach for ので.

That's the whole trick: ので is から's gentler twin, plain form in front, な glued onto nouns. Hold onto this reason-first shape — it's the same instinct you'll lean on soon when we start ordering events in time with てから ("after doing").
caution_notes: With nouns and な-adjectives, use な before ので (医者なので), never だ — 学生ので is wrong.
The reason clause with ので comes first, and ので attaches to the plain form even when the sentence ends politely.
ので frames the reason as objective fact, so prefer から under strong commands or blunt opinions.
In casual speech ので often contracts to んで with the same meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're describing your morning to a friend, and you want to say two things that happened in a row: you woke up, and then you ate breakfast. In English you'd just drop an "and" between them. In Japanese, you don't reach for a word that means "and" — you bend the first verb into a new shape called the て形[けい] (te-form), and that shape does the connecting for you.

Watch it link two actions into one smooth sentence:

```jp
起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*I wake up and eat breakfast.*

The first verb 起[お]きる became 起[お]きて, and that little て is doing all the work of "and then." The second verb stays polite and normal (食[た]べます), carrying the tense for the whole sentence. That's the core idea: the て形[けい] is a connector that hands the tense and politeness off to whatever comes after it.

## How it works

The て形[けい] (the connective form — the shape a verb takes when it needs to hook onto something) is built from the plain dictionary form of the verb. How you build it depends on which group the verb belongs to.

**Ichidan verbs** (the "る-droppers", like 食[た]べる and 見[み]る) are the easy ones. Drop the る, add て. That's it.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて
```

*to eat → eating / eat and…*

So 見[み]る becomes 見[み]て, 起[お]きる becomes 起[お]きて, 寝[ね]る becomes 寝[ね]て. One clean rule, no surprises.

**Godan verbs** are messier, because the ending sound changes depending on the last kana. This is the part everyone has to drill, so here's the whole map:

- く → いて (書[か]く → 書[か]いて)
- ぐ → いで (the voiced version keeps its voicing: で, not て)
- ぶ・む・ぬ → んで (飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで, 遊[あそ]ぶ → 遊[あそ]んで)
- す → して (話[はな]す → 話[はな]して)
- う・つ・る → って (買[か]う → 買[か]って, 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]って, 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]って)

Here's the intuition, not just the chart: the sounds cluster by what's easy to say. The nasal-ish endings (ぶ・む・ぬ) all collapse into んで, and the "small tongue-tap" endings (う・つ・る) all collapse into って. You're not memorizing five random rules — you're memorizing three sound families.

```jp
書[か]いて
飲[の]んで
待[ま]って
```

*writing / drinking / waiting (all te-form)*

**The irregulars** are just two verbs, and you already know both. 来[く]る becomes 来[らい]て, and する becomes して. 行[い]く looks godan but breaks the く→いて rule — it goes to 行[い]って, not `行いて`. That one exception bites everyone, so tuck it away now.

Put it all together and you can chain a whole morning:

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*Every morning I get up and eat breakfast.*

Notice again: only the *last* verb is 食[た]べます. Everything before it rides on the て形[けい], and the politeness plus the tense live entirely in that final verb.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest thing to understand: **the て形[けい] carries no tense and no politeness by itself.** It's a hinge. Whether the sentence is polite or plain, present or past, is decided by the verb at the very end.

That means to talk about the past, you don't touch the て形[けい] at all — you only change the final verb.

```jp
起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べました。
```

*I got up and ate breakfast.*

Same 起[お]きて as before. Only 食[た]べます turned into 食[た]べました, and suddenly the whole thing is in the past. The て form never conjugates for tense — resist the urge to invent a past te-form.

> 行[い]く → 行[い]って is the one you'll get wrong. By the く→いて rule you'd expect `行いて`, but it isn't. It's 行[い]って, patterning with the う・つ・る family instead.

One more constraint: don't use ます-form before the て. Learners fresh off the polite endings sometimes write `食べますて`. That's not a thing. The て attaches to the plain verb stem, never to ます.

## Casual speech

The te-form itself doesn't contract much, but it has one very common everyday job: it becomes a soft command or request on its own. Said with a rising, gentle tone, a bare て形[けい] means "do this, please" in casual speech.

```jp
起[お]きて。
```

*Get up. / Wake up. (casual, spoken to someone close)*

You'd say this to a family member who's oversleeping, not to your boss. It's warm and informal. The fuller polite request form is coming later, but this stripped-down version is what you'll actually hear at home.

## Contrast

You already know ます, ました, and ません — the polite endings that finish a sentence and lock in the tense. The te-form lives in a completely different spot: it never finishes a sentence (except the casual command above), it *connects* to more.

Compare a sentence that stops after one action with one that chains two:

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*Every morning I eat breakfast.*

That's complete — ます closes it. Now put an action *before* it, and the earlier verb has to become て形[けい] to make room:

```jp
昨日[きのう]起[お]きて、コーヒーを飲[の]みました。
```

*Yesterday I got up and drank coffee.*

The final verb 飲[の]みました handles "yesterday" and the past tense for both actions. 起[お]きて just links in front of it. Swap the final verb's ending — to 飲[の]みます, 飲[の]みません — and you've changed the whole sentence's tense or polarity without ever retouching 起[お]きて. That's the division of labor: **te-form connects, the final verb decides.**

Hold onto this. Once you meet the plain past た形[かたち] soon, you'll notice the te-form and the ta-form are built from nearly the same sound rules — learn て cleanly now and た comes almost free.

That's the whole pattern: bend the earlier verb to て形[けい], let the last verb carry tense and politeness, and you can string your day together in one breath.
caution_notes: The te-form carries no tense or politeness itself — the final verb in the sentence decides both.
行く is irregular: it becomes 行って, not the expected 行いて.
Never attach て to a ます-form; it hooks onto the plain verb (食べて, not 食べますて).
For godan verbs, group the endings by sound: ぶ・む・ぬ → んで and う・つ・る → って.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place in Tokyo, and the tea on the table smells amazing. You want a cup, but it's not yours to just grab. In English you'd ask "can I have some?" — in Japanese you reach for てもいい, the pattern that asks *is it okay if I…?*

```jp
このお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]んでもいいですか。
```

*Is it okay if I drink this tea?*

That's the whole job of てもいい: you describe an action, then ask whether doing it is permitted — or, without the question, you *grant* that permission to someone else. It's the polite handshake around "may I" and "you may."

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own the hard part. Take a verb, put it into its て-form (the same form you learned for てください and ている), then bolt on もいい.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → 食[た]べてもいい
```

*eat → eating(-form) → may eat*

The literal pieces are worth seeing once. も means *even*, and いい means *good*. So 食[た]べてもいい is *even if I eat, it's good* — "even doing this is fine," which is exactly how permission feels. That's your *why*: the も is what makes it *permission* rather than a command.

To make it polite, add です on the end. Both of these are correct; the first is plain, the second is the one you'll say to a stranger or a teacher.

```jp
ここに座[すわ]ってもいい。
ここに座[すわ]ってもいいですか。
```

*I may sit here. / Is it okay if I sit here?*

When you're the one *giving* permission, drop the question and just state it. A parent to a child, a host to a guest:

```jp
テレビを見[み]てもいいですよ。
```

*You may watch TV.*

There's also a more formal, more generous-sounding variant: てもかまいません, literally *even doing it, I don't mind*. Use it when you want to sound extra accommodating — a station attendant, say, telling you it's no trouble.

```jp
ここで待[ま]ってもかまいません。
```

*You may wait here (I don't mind at all).*

## Rules and exceptions

The most common early mistake is dropping the も. Learners hear that permission is "て + いい" and write `食べていい` thinking that's the neutral form. In casual speech that contraction does happen (more on that below), but in careful, polite Japanese the も carries the *permission* meaning — leave it out in a formal setting and it sounds unfinished. When in doubt, keep the も.

> てもいい asks about *your own* action or grants one to someone else. It does **not** work as a general "is X allowed here?" sign-style rule. For that broader "is it forbidden?" feeling you'll want a different pattern (coming very soon).

Another sharp edge: adding か makes it a genuine request for permission, and the answer matters. If you ask 飲[の]んでもいいですか and the host says だめ (no good), you don't drink. Without か, you're not asking — you're telling someone it's fine. Mixing those up can make you sound like you're granting yourself permission out loud, which is a little odd.

One more: because いい is an adjective, some learners try to bend it like `食べてもいかった` for the past. Don't chase that at N5 — stick to the present *may / it's okay* meaning, which covers almost every situation you'll meet.

## Casual speech

Among friends, two things happen. First, the polite です falls away. Second — and this is the big one — the も itself often contracts out, so てもいい becomes ていい in fast speech.

```jp
これ食[た]べてもいい。
これ食[た]べていい。
```

*Can I eat this? (both casual)*

Both are casual and both are fine between friends; the second, with the も gone, is the more relaxed of the two. The tone alone (a rising, questioning tone) does the work that か does in polite speech.

> Keep the も in anything written, formal, or spoken to someone above you. The dropped-も version is friends-and-family territory only.

## Contrast

You've met てください — *please do this* — and it lives right next door, because both attach to the て-form. But they point in opposite directions. てください *asks the other person to act*; てもいい asks whether *you* may act, or tells the other person they *may*.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてください。
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてもいいですか。
```

*Please open the window. / Is it okay if I open the window?*

The first hands the job to your listener. The second keeps the action with you and just checks permission. Swap one for the other and you've flipped who's doing the opening — a real change in meaning, not just politeness.

It's also worth setting てもいい beside ませんか, the invitation you learned. ませんか pulls the other person into an activity with you — *won't you…?* — while てもいい is purely about whether an action is allowed.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]きませんか。
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]ってもいいですか。
```

*Won't you go together (with me)? / Is it okay if I come along?*

The first is a warm invitation you extend; the second is you asking to be let in. Same activity, completely different social move.

Here's the one-line recap: て-form + もいい asks or grants permission — *may I / you may*. Hold onto the shape, because the moment you can say "you may," the natural next question is "and what may I *not* do?" — that's てはいけない, *must not*, waiting for you just around the corner.
caution_notes: In polite Japanese keep the も — dropping it (食べていい) is casual only and sounds unfinished in formal speech.
Add か to ask for permission; without か you are granting permission, not requesting it.
てもいい asks about your own action or grants one to someone else — it is not a general 'is X allowed here?' rule sign.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in a quiet library, and your friend pulls out their phone to make a call. Before they even tap the screen, you want to stop them — not with a polite "please don't," but with the flat, no-exceptions "you can't do that here." That's the job of てはいけない.

This is the pattern for rules and prohibitions: the sign on the wall, the thing the teacher says, the line you don't cross. It's the mirror image of something you already know — てもいい, which grants permission. Where てもいい opens a door, てはいけない slams it shut.

```jp
ここで電[でん]話[わ]を使[つか]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not use the phone here.*

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own half of it. Take a verb, put it in its て-form (the same て-form you use for てください and てもいい), and attach はいけない. That's the whole machine.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → 食[た]べてはいけない
飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで → 飲[の]んではいけない
```

*eat → (te-form) → must not eat*
*drink → (te-form) → must not drink*

The polite version just swaps いけない for いけません. Same meaning, more formal register — the kind of thing you'd see on a posted notice or hear from station staff.

```jp
ここでお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
```

*You must not drink alcohol here.*

Why はいけない? Literally いけない is a word meaning "it won't do" or "it's no good." So the whole thing reads like "doing X won't do." That's a useful intuition: you're not commanding a person directly, you're declaring that a certain *action* is not acceptable. The は in the middle is the topic particle — it's marking "as for doing this thing" — which is exactly why it's pronounced *wa*, not *ha*.

```jp
夜[よる]にコーヒーを飲[の]んではいけない。
```

*You must not drink coffee at night.*

## Rules and exceptions

The て-form does the heavy lifting, so every irregular て-form you've already met carries straight over. 行[い]く becomes 行[い]って (not `行きて`), 話[はな]す becomes 話[はな]して, 待[ま]つ becomes 待[ま]って. If your て-form is right, the prohibition is right.

```jp
その部屋[へや]に入[はい]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not enter that room.*

One thing to watch: because いけない ends like a negative, learners sometimes try to negate it again to say "don't have to." That's a different pattern entirely, and stacking negatives here just produces something broken. Don't reach for `食べてはいけなくない` — it isn't a thing.

> てはいけない is genuinely strong. It's the register of laws, safety signs, and adults laying down rules to children. Saying it to your host at a dinner party — even about something small — lands like scolding. For softening someone's behavior gently, this is the wrong tool.

The subject is usually left unspoken, because a prohibition tends to apply to everyone or to "you." But you can name who's bound by the rule with は or が when you need to be clear about it.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
```

*Children must not drink alcohol.*

## Casual speech

In real conversation, てはいけない contracts hard. The ては collapses into ちゃ, so 食[た]べてはいけない becomes 食[た]べちゃいけない. This is everywhere in casual speech — friends, family, anyone you'd already be speaking plainly with.

```jp
それを食[た]べちゃいけない。
```

*You can't eat that.*

The で-form verbs (the ones whose て-form is で, like 飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで) shift to じゃ instead: 飲[の]んではいけない → 飲[の]んじゃいけない. Same logic, just following the voicing of the sound before it.

```jp
今[いま]、帰[かえ]っちゃいけない。
```

*You can't go home right now.*

Even the ending often gets trimmed — people drop off after ちゃ and just let the tone or a trailing だめ carry the "no good" meaning. But for now, ちゃいけない is the reliable casual form to lock in.

## Contrast

Line てはいけない up against てもいい, the permission pattern you learned right before it. They share the て-form base and differ only in the tail, but they're opposites — and that's the cleanest way to feel the meaning.

```jp
ここで写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]てはいけません。
```

*You must not look at photos here.*

```jp
ここで写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]てもいいです。
```

*You may look at photos here.*

One tail says "no," the other says "yes." If you can build one, you can build the other — same verb, same て-form, just choose the door.

It's also worth separating this from てください, your request pattern. てください asks someone to *do* something as a favor; てはいけない tells them an action is *off-limits* as a rule. "Please close the door" and "you must not close the door" are not two shades of the same idea — one is a polite ask, the other is a prohibition.

So: て-form plus はいけない is your "off-limits" stamp, softening to ちゃいけない among friends. When you later want to say "please *don't*" as a gentle request rather than a hard rule, you'll meet ないでください — a much softer way to hold someone back, and the natural next step from here.
caution_notes: Build it from the て-form: 行く → 行って → 行ってはいけない, never 行きて.
The は in てはいけない is pronounced wa, not ha, because it's the topic particle.
てはいけない is strong — the register of rules and signs; it lands as scolding in casual polite situations.
In casual speech ては contracts to ちゃ (食べちゃいけない) and で-verbs use じゃ (飲んじゃいけない).

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a party and someone mentions they just got back from Japan. You want to say "Oh, I've been to Japan too!" — not "I'm going," not "I went yesterday," but the bigger thing: *this is part of my life experience.* Japanese has a dedicated shape for exactly that, and it's built from parts you already own.

Here's the move:

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがあります。
```

*I have been to Japan.*

That last chunk, ことがあります, is the whole trick. Literally it's saying "the fact of having gone exists" — and once you hear it that way, it stops feeling like a weird idiom and starts feeling logical.

## How it works

You take a verb, put it in its plain past form (the た-form, the casual "did" version), and then bolt on ことがある.

The recipe is always the same:

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べた → 食[た]べたことがある
```

*eat → ate → have eaten (before)*

Let's break down that tail. こと is a nominalizer — a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a *thing* you can talk about. So 食[た]べた ("ate") becomes 食[た]べたこと ("the experience of having eaten"). Then が marks it as the subject, and ある means "exists." Put together: "the experience of having eaten exists." That's your "I have eaten before."

So the two halves you're managing are the た-form on the left and the fixed ことがある on the right. If your た-form is right, you're done.

```jp
私[わたし]はあの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]たことがあります。
```

*I have seen that movie before.*

```jp
彼[かれ]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んだことがあります。
```

*He has drunk alcohol before.*

Notice the polite ending lives all the way at the end: あります for polite, ある for plain. The verb in front stays in casual past no matter how polite you're being — that's normal, and it trips people up the first week. The politeness of the whole sentence is decided by that final ある / あります, not by the た-form.

To ask about experience, just add か, same as any polite question:

```jp
日本[にほん]の料[りょう]理[り]を食[た]べたことがありますか。
```

*Have you ever eaten Japanese food?*

## Rules and exceptions

The big one: this pattern is about *life experience*, not about "one specific time in the recent past." If you did something yesterday, you use plain past (食[た]べた), not this. Save ことがある for "at some point in my life, this has happened."

> Don't use たことがある for things you literally just did or do routinely. "I ate breakfast this morning" is 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べました, not 食[た]べたことがあります — the experience frame would sound like you're marveling that breakfast has ever occurred in your life.

To say you *haven't* ever done something, you make the ある negative — turn あります into ありません (or ある into ない in plain speech). The verb in front stays exactly the same.

```jp
私[わたし]はまだこの魚[さかな]を食[た]べたことがありません。
```

*I have never eaten this fish yet.*

A common wrong guess is to negate the verb instead of ある — learners write things like `食べないことがあります`, which means something totally different ("there are times I don't eat"). Keep the verb positive and past; move the negation to the very end.

> The negative goes on ある, never on the front verb. 食[た]べたことがありません = "have never eaten." `食べなかったことがある` is a real but rare and confusing shape — as a beginner, don't reach for it.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, two things happen. First, the polite tail drops to plain: あります becomes ある, ありません becomes ない. Second — and this is the one you'll hear constantly — the が simply gets dropped.

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがある。
```

*I've been to Japan.*

Drop the が and you get the everyday spoken version:

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことある。
```

*I've been to Japan. (casual)*

Both are fine in casual speech; the が-less one just sounds more like talking than writing. For the negative, ない does the same job: 見[み]たことない means "never seen it." When you're writing or being polite, keep the が and use あります.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is plain ている — the ongoing-state pattern (Verb-て + いる). It's worth lining these up because both can touch the past, but they point in opposite directions.

ている tells you about a *current* state or an action in progress right now:

```jp
彼[かれ]は今[いま]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べています。
```

*He is eating a meal right now.*

たことがある tells you about a *past experience* that colors the present:

```jp
彼[かれ]はこの料[りょう]理[り]を食[た]べたことがあります。
```

*He has eaten this dish before.*

Swap one for the other and the meaning flips completely: 食[た]べています is "eating now," 食[た]べたことがあります is "has eaten at some point in life." One is a live camera, the other is a résumé line.

It's also worth separating this from the plain past you already use. 見[み]た is "saw (a specific time)"; 見[み]たことがある is "have seen (ever)." If a friend asks どの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]た — "which movie did you watch?" — they mean last night. If they ask あの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]たことがある, they mean "in your whole life, ever?"

Hold onto the こと nominalizer here — that trick of turning a verb into a thing shows up again soon, and the た-form muscle you're building will pay off directly when we meet たり〜たりする for listing actions.

Recap: verb in casual past + ことがある = "have done it before." Negate the ある, not the verb, and drop the が when you're being casual.
caution_notes: Use たことがある for life experience, not for something you just did — 'I ate breakfast this morning' is 食べました, not 食べたことがあります.
Negate the ある (ありません / ない), never the front verb; the verb stays in casual past.
In casual speech the polite tail drops to ある/ない and が is often omitted (行ったことある).

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place and they've been coughing all evening. You want to say, gently, "you should go to the hospital." Not a command, not "you must" — just solid, caring advice. That's exactly the job of ほうがいい.

The pattern means something like *had better* or *should*. You attach it to a verb and you're handing someone a recommendation: this choice is the better one. Here's the hospital line.

```jp
病[びょう]院[いん]に行[い]ったほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should go to the hospital.*

Notice the verb is 行[い]った — the past form — even though nothing has happened yet. That surprises everyone at first. Hold that thought; it's the whole trick of this pattern.

## How it works

There are two shapes, depending on whether you're recommending *doing* something or *not doing* it.

For "you should do X", take the plain past form of the verb (the た-form) and add ほうがいい.

```jp
薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだほうがいいです。
今日[きょう]は休[やす]んだほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should take medicine.*
*You should rest today.*

Why the past form for future advice? Think of ほう as "the ~ side / the ~ option" (it's the same 方[ほう] you'll meet in comparisons). You're literally saying "the *having-taken-medicine* side is good" — you picture the action as already done and judge that outcome as the better one. The past form freezes the action into a completed picture you can weigh.

For "you should *not* do X", use the plain negative — the ない-form — and add ほうがいい. This one stays present, no past trickery.

```jp
そのお酒[さけ]を飲[の]まないほうがいいです。
今日[きょう]は泳[およ]がないほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not drink that alcohol.*
*You'd better not swim today.*

So the split is clean: **positive advice → past (た) + ほうがいい**, **negative advice → ない + ほうがいい**. That asymmetry looks odd but it's fixed and reliable.

You can make the whole thing more polite by keeping です on the end (ほうがいいです), or leave it off for plain speech (ほうがいい). And you can soften it further by tacking よ on the end, which makes it feel like a friendly heads-up rather than a verdict.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest trap is reaching for the plain *present* form on the positive side. 行[い]くほうがいい isn't the natural advice pattern — for a specific recommendation to a specific person, you want 行[い]ったほうがいい.

> For concrete, in-the-moment advice ("you should go *now*"), use the past form: 行[い]ったほうがいい. The present form 行[い]くほうがいい drifts toward general comparison ("going is the better option, in general") and sounds weaker as personal advice.

The negative side has no such split — it's always ない, never past.

```jp
たくさん食[た]べないほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not eat a lot.*

One more thing about tone: ほうがいい is genuinely stronger than a bare suggestion. When you say 休[やす]んだほうがいい, you're implying there's a real downside to *not* resting. For a lighter "how about resting?" you'd reach for something else entirely (you already know どうですか for that). Save ほうがいい for when you mean it.

## Casual speech

Drop the です and you're already casual: 飲[の]んだほうがいい. In fast speech people often shorten ほう to ほ and swallow the が, so ほうがいい can come out sounding like *ほうがいい* run together — you'll hear it, you don't need to produce it. The safe casual form is simply the plain one with よ:

```jp
早[はや]く寝[ね]たほうがいいよ。
```

*You'd better go to sleep early.*

That よ is doing a lot of work — it turns a flat statement into "hey, just so you know." Very common when you're looking out for a friend.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is かもしれない, *might / maybe*. They feel related but do opposite jobs. かもしれない reports a possibility; ほうがいい pushes a choice.

```jp
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]かもしれません。
傘[かさ]を持[も]ったほうがいいですよ。
```

*It might rain tomorrow.*
*You'd better take an umbrella.*

See how the first sentence just floats a possibility, and the second one leans in with a recommendation because of it. Swap them and it breaks: you can't advise with かもしれない, and ほうがいい can't merely speculate.

It also brushes up against と思[おも]う, *I think that*. と思[おも]う is your private opinion; ほうがいい is a recommendation aimed at the listener. "この本[ほん]はいいと思[おも]う" says what *you* feel; "この本[ほん]を読[よ]んだほうがいい" tells the other person what to *do*. Same warmth, different direction.

## Closing

Recap: past (た) form for "you should," ない form for "you'd better not," both capped with ほうがいい — and add です or よ to set the tone. The past-tense-for-future-advice quirk is the one to burn in.

Hold onto the ない side of this pattern — that plain negative form is the same building block you'll need soon when we meet まだ〜ていない, "haven't done it yet."
caution_notes: For positive advice use the plain past (た) form: 行ったほうがいい, not 行くほうがいい.
For negative advice always use the plain negative (ない) form — never a past form.
ほうがいい is stronger than a casual suggestion; it implies a real downside to ignoring it, so save it for when you mean it.
Add です for politeness or よ for a friendly heads-up; the bare plain form is casual.
